teaser: An apple tree that also grows grapes, a puzzled Adam, and a snake hidden twice.
review_notes:
Dimensions given as 117 x 80 cm (Courtauld figure is about 117.1 x 80.8 cm).
Cranach as witness at Luther's wedding (1525) and godfather to his first child (1526): standard biography, worth a check.
'More than fifty' surviving Adam and Eve pictures from Cranach and his workshop: commonly cited figure.
Change of the serpent's wings after the death of Hans Cranach in 1537: standard account.
Reading of the grapevine as a sign of redemption follows the Courtauld's own interpretation.
The photo includes the inner edge of the frame on all four sides.

lesson.text: This picture is not on canvas. It is painted on a wooden panel about 117 cm high and 80 cm wide (46 x 31 in), planed smooth and coated with a chalk ground. That hard, even surface is why the paint looks almost like enamel: every leaf has an edge, every apple a small shine.

The year is 1526, the town is Wittenberg in Saxony, and the painter is Lucas Cranach the Elder, court artist to the local princes. He is in his fifties and runs one of the busiest workshops in Germany. The subject is the oldest story he knows: the first man, the first woman, and one piece of fruit.
The third character of the story is here too, quiet and well camouflaged. Where is the serpent?

spots.title: The serpent
spots.text: It slides down the pale trunk in an S, its gray-blue scales close to the color of the bark. Its head hangs just above the couple, turned toward Eve's side.

lesson.text: So the snake has already done its talking. Cranach picks the second after: Eve has picked the apple and is passing it across the trunk. In the Book of Genesis this is the moment before everything goes wrong, when humans are still at home in the garden.
Most painters make this scene solemn. Cranach makes it a little funny. Adam does not look tempted or afraid. He looks like someone asked a question he cannot quite answer.

lesson.title: A slow decision
lesson.text: Follow the handover from his head to her arm.

spots.title: Scratching his head
spots.text: Adam's left hand is buried in his curls. It is the universal gesture of doubt, and it is rare in paintings of this subject.

spots.title: Two hands, one apple
spots.text: Her fingers are still on the fruit and his are closing under it. Nobody has bitten yet. The whole story hangs on this small red circle.

spots.title: Eve's glance
spots.text: She watches him from the corner of her eye with a faint smile. She seems to know his answer before he does.

spots.title: A hand on the branch
spots.text: Her other arm reaches up to hold the bough the apple came from. One long line runs from the tree, through her body, to Adam's hand.

lesson.text: Now notice the bodies themselves. In Italy at this time, painters built nudes from muscle and Greek statues. Cranach goes another way: narrow shoulders, long legs, pale skin with almost no shadow, set like cutouts against dark bushes. People still recognize a Cranach figure from across a room.
Painting was only one of Cranach's businesses. He owned a pharmacy in Wittenberg, held a license to sell wine, ran a printing press, and was elected mayor of the town several times.

Around the couple, the garden is crowded. Cranach knew animals well, because he painted the hunts of the Saxon court. Here, though, nobody is hunting anybody. Predators and prey share the same grass, which is his way of saying: this is still Paradise.

spots.title: The lion
spots.text: It crouches with its eyes on you, not on the deer a step away. In Eden the lion has no reason to pounce.

spots.title: The wild boar
spots.text: A dark, bristly boar noses through the grass above the lion. At court it was dangerous game. Here it is just a neighbor.

spots.title: The white horse
spots.text: Far back in the meadow a small white horse rears up. It is the only animal in motion, a flash of energy in a very still picture.

spots.title: The stag
spots.text: A big stag lies in front, and its antlers rise right across Adam's legs. Cranach uses them, along with a leafy twig, to keep the scene decent.

spots.title: The sheep
spots.text: Two sheep rest behind the stag, one with its head down in the grass. Meek animals sit closest to Adam.

spots.title: The stork
spots.text: A stork stands at the very front, between the couple's feet, painted feather by feather in black, white and gray.

spots.title: Deer at the water
spots.text: A pair of roe deer come to the pool. One lowers its head to drink, and a heron waits in the water just to the right.

spots.title: The partridges
spots.text: Two plump little birds peck at the bank of the pool. Their brown feathers nearly vanish against the mud.

lesson.text: This was a bestseller. More than fifty paintings of Adam and Eve survive from Cranach and his workshop, each a little different. Assistants worked from the master's models, which let the shop deliver pictures faster than almost any rival.
There is one plant in this garden that makes no botanical sense, and it is the most thoughtful detail in the painting. It sits right on the trunk, between the two bodies.
This is an apple tree. Yet another kind of fruit hangs from it. Can you spot it?

spots.title: Grapes
spots.text: A vine climbs the trunk, with dark bunches of grapes at hip height and jagged vine leaves. Apples above, grapes below, on one and the same tree.

lesson.text: For Christians, grapes mean wine, and wine means the blood of Christ, shed to repair what the apple broke. Cranach puts the cure on the same tree as the fault. The fall is about to happen, and the rescue is already growing.

Cranach was a close friend of Martin Luther, who lived in the same town. He was a witness at Luther's wedding in 1525 and godfather to his first child, and his portraits made the reformer's face known across Europe.
One thing is still missing: a name. Cranach did not sign with letters. He used a small emblem taken from the coat of arms a prince had granted him in 1508, and he placed it here with a wink.

lesson.title: Two snakes
lesson.text: The painter's mark is on the trunk, a short way below the real serpent.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: A tiny pale mark on the bark: the date 1526 and, under it, a little winged serpent holding a ring. This emblem served as the trademark of the whole workshop.

spots.title: The other serpent
spots.text: Just above, the tempter's head hangs off the branch. In a picture about a snake, Cranach signs with a snake, and puts the two almost nose to nose.

lesson.text: The little serpent changed over time. In early works its wings stand upright, like a bat's. After Cranach's son Hans died in 1537, the wings were painted folded down, like a bird's. Experts use this to help date the pictures.
Cranach tells the fall of man as a quiet comedy in a peaceful zoo, then hides its serious point in a bunch of grapes: the remedy grows on the same tree as the mistake.
The panel now hangs in the Courtauld Gallery in London, and Adam is still scratching his head. Five centuries on, he has not taken the bite. Would you tell him to hand it back?

quiz.question: What is this picture painted on?
quiz.explanation: It is a wooden panel coated with a smooth chalk ground, which gives the enamel-like finish.

quiz.question: What is Adam doing while he takes the apple?
quiz.explanation: His left hand is in his curls, a gesture of doubt.

quiz.question: What does the grapevine on the apple tree stand for?
options: The blood of Christ, a promise of rescue
quiz.explanation: Grapes mean wine and the blood of Christ, the cure placed beside the fault.

quiz.question: How did Cranach sign the painting?
options: With his full name on a scroll
With a small winged serpent on the trunk
With his portrait among the animals
quiz.explanation: His emblem, a winged serpent with a ring, sits on the bark with the date 1526.

quiz.question: Why do the lion and the deer lie side by side?
options: They show that this is still Paradise
They are trophies of a court hunt
quiz.explanation: Before the fall, predators and prey live in peace.

quiz.question: Which famous neighbor was a close friend of Cranach?
quiz.explanation: Cranach was a witness at Luther's wedding and painted his portraits.

facts.text: Cranach's workshop painted Adam and Eve only once.
facts.explanation: More than fifty versions survive from Cranach and his workshop.

facts.text: Besides painting, Cranach owned a pharmacy and served as mayor of Wittenberg.
facts.explanation: He ran several businesses and was elected mayor more than once.

facts.text: In this painting, Adam has already bitten into the apple.
facts.explanation: The fruit is still whole, held between his hand and Eve's.
